title: Vertical and Directional Metaphors: Center vs. Periphery

sections.title: The Vertical Metaphor: fel Budapestre vs. le vidékre
sections.content: Hungarian conceptualizes movement between the capital and the provinces through deeply ingrained vertical metaphors. Traveling toward Budapest is culturally and linguistically marked as ascending: 'felmegy a fővárosba' ('goes up to the capital'), 'felutazik Pestre'. Moving away from the capital into regional towns or rural areas is framed as descending: 'lemegy vidékre' ('goes down to the countryside'), 'leutazik Szegedre'. This reflects historical administrative centralization and railway networks converging on Budapest.

sections.title: Containment vs. Open Space: be vs. ki
sections.content: Complementing the vertical axis is an enclosure dynamic: moving into a town center or institutional core uses 'be' ('beköltözik a centrumba'), whereas dispersing into agricultural open spaces uses 'ki' ('kiköltözik a tanyára' - 'moves out to the farmstead', 'kijár a határba' - 'goes out to the fields'). Sociologically, these directional cues encode status, urbanization, and peripheral marginalization.

items.english: Settlements on the economic periphery struggle to connect into the central bloodstream.

sections.title: B2 Stylistic Notice
sections.content: Even when traveling south to Szeged or Pécs from Budapest, one still says 'lemegy' (down to the country) rather than 'délre megy' in colloquial Hungarian, while coming to Budapest is always 'felutazik' regardless of compass direction.
